value.overview: The Scale-crested Pygmy-Tyrant (Lophotriccus pileatus) is a tiny, active tyrant flycatcher of humid forests in Central and northern South America. It is named for the short, scale-like crown feathers that can form a small crest when the bird is alert. Despite its size, it often draws attention with sharp calls and energetic movements. In Costa Rica, it is a resident of forested foothills and lower mountain regions, where it may be easier to hear than see.
value.classification: The species belongs to the tyrant flycatcher family, Tyrannidae, and the small group of pygmy-tyrants in the genus Lophotriccus. Several geographic forms are recognized across its broad, discontinuous range.
value.identification: This very small flycatcher has olive-green upperparts, a short tail, and pale underparts marked with fine dusky streaking on the throat and breast. Its most distinctive feature is the crown, where elongated dark feathers have pale or rufous edges and create a scaled appearance. The bill is short and broad, and the bird often flicks through dense vegetation. In Costa Rica, it can be confused with other tiny forest flycatchers, so its crown pattern, streaked underparts, calls, and habitat are useful clues.
value.rangeHabitat: The Scale-crested Pygmy-Tyrant occurs from southeastern Honduras and Nicaragua through Costa Rica and Panama, with additional populations in Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador, Peru, and Bolivia. In Costa Rica, it is found on both slopes, especially in humid foothills and lower montane zones; it occurs along much of the Caribbean slope and on the Pacific slope from the central region southward. It uses humid to wet evergreen forest, cloud forest, mature secondary growth, forest edges, and natural gaps, generally from low elevations into the foothills.
value.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica and across most or all of its range. It is not regarded as a regular long-distance migrant, although local movements may occur in response to conditions or elevation.
value.breeding: The breeding season is not fully defined, and specific timing for Costa Rica remains poorly documented; nesting activity elsewhere in the range includes March through June. The nest is a domed, hanging bag with a side entrance protected by a small awning. It is woven from plant fibers, often with loose material dangling below, and suspended from a twig several meters above the ground. The clutch is two eggs, and the female is thought to perform the incubation; incubation and fledging periods are not well known.
value.dietFeeding: It feeds mainly on small insects and other arthropods captured from foliage. The bird usually forages in dense understory and lower to middle vegetation, moving actively among leaves and twigs and making short flights to seize prey. It may search forest edges, vine tangles, gaps, and secondary growth as well as mature forest. Its small size and unobtrusive feeding style can make it difficult to locate even when it is calling nearby.
value.behavior: Scale-crested Pygmy-Tyrants are active, alert birds that often remain within dense vegetation. They commonly forage singly or in pairs and may join mixed-species feeding flocks with other small insect-eating birds. The crown feathers can be raised during excitement, territorial interactions, or alarm. Their sharp, repeated calls are often the best way to detect them. In Costa Rica, observers frequently hear the species before obtaining a clear view in shaded foothill forest.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is not well quantified, but the species remains widespread and is not currently considered globally threatened.
